title: Unauthorized Access to Live GPS Data
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) stores and processes live GPS coordinates transmitted from the child's device. Without proper access controls, unauthorized actors could access this sensitive location data, potentially revealing the child's real-time movements and whereabouts.
assumptions: Backend has access control vulnerabilities or insufficient authentication mechanisms

title: Excessive Location Data Collection
description: Live GPS coordinates transmitted at regular intervals may constitute data minimization violations. Continuous tracking could collect more location data than necessary for the stated purpose, potentially violating privacy-by-design principles and data minimization requirements.
assumptions: The stated purpose does not require continuous real-time tracking

title: Location-Based Identification of Child
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) processes GPS coordinates that could be used to identify the child's specific location, movements, and patterns. This data could be combined with other information to uniquely identify the child, creating identification risks.
assumptions: GPS data can be correlated with other identifiers

title: Linkability of GPS Data to Other Records
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) could link the live GPS coordinates to other data about the child (e.g., personal information, other activities), creating a comprehensive profile of the child's movements and behaviors that could be misused.
assumptions: Backend has access to other child-related data

title: Regulatory Non-Compliance for Location Tracking
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) may face regulatory non-compliance issues regarding child location tracking. Laws like GDPR, COPPA, and other child privacy regulations have specific requirements for collecting and processing location data of minors.
assumptions: Applicable privacy regulations require explicit consent and data protection measures

title: Unnecessary Location Data Storage
description: Backend writes each location ping to the Location History Store, potentially storing more location data than strictly necessary for the intended purpose. This violates the minimality principle - only location data required for the specific functionality should be retained.
assumptions: Location data is personal data; storing it creates a privacy risk if not absolutely necessary.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 from context [5] as it describes data disclosure across boundaries. The exact tree node may vary in LINDDUN Pro.

title: Location History Linkability
description: Stored location history can be linked to identify individuals and their movement patterns over time. Sequential location data creates a detailed profile of user behavior and routines.
assumptions: Location data is personally identifiable; sequential data enables pattern recognition.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability threats in LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Location Data Identifiability
description: Location pings can be used to identify individuals, their home/work locations, and frequent destinations. Even without explicit identifiers, location patterns can reveal personal information.
assumptions: Location data is inherently identifiable; patterns can be used to infer personal information.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for identifiability threats in LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Unintended Location Data Disclosure to Geofencing Engine
description: Location pings containing personal location data are transferred from Mobile App Backend to Geofencing Engine. This disclosure may be avoidable if the geofencing engine can operate with less granular location information (e.g., zone IDs instead of precise coordinates), or if the transfer is not strictly necessary for the stated purpose.
assumptions: Location data is personal data; the geofencing engine has access to this data; the transfer is not encrypted or access-controlled
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure; the exact tree node may vary in LINDDUN Pro

title: Geofencing Engine Receives Personal Location Data
description: The Geofencing Engine receives and processes personal location data from the backend. This represents a data disclosure boundary where personal data is transferred to a system component that may have broader access than necessary.
assumptions: The geofencing engine is a separate system component; location data is considered personal data
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure; the exact tree node may vary in LINDDUN Pro

title: Location Data Used for User Identification
description: Location pings transferred to the Geofencing Engine could be used to identify or track specific users, potentially enabling profiling or surveillance beyond the intended geofencing functionality.
assumptions: Location data can be correlated with user identity; the geofencing engine has access to user identification information
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable identification threat node; exact node may vary in LINDDUN Pro

title: Location Data Integrity Compromised During Transfer
description: Location pings transferred from Backend to Geofencing Engine could be tampered with, leading to incorrect geofencing decisions (e.g., false zone entry/exit alerts).
assumptions: The transfer channel is not fully secured; the geofencing engine relies on accurate location data
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as a reasonable data integrity threat node; exact node may vary in LINDDUN Pro

title: Linkability of Zone Definitions to Family Members
description: Zone definitions (home, school, friend's house) stored in DS2 could be linked to specific family members through metadata, timestamps, or access patterns, potentially revealing which family member uses which location.
assumptions: Zone definitions may contain or be associated with family member identifiers or usage patterns that enable linking.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability threats in DataStore context

title: Identification of Family Members via Location Data
description: Zone definitions stored in DS2 could be used to identify family members' locations, routines, and associations (e.g., school, friend's house), potentially enabling inference of personal information.
assumptions: Zone definitions are associated with family members and could be accessed or inferred by unauthorized parties.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for identification threats in DataStore context

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Zone Definitions
description: Zone definitions in DS2 could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through improper access controls, data leaks, or insecure transmission to P2, revealing sensitive location information about family members.
assumptions: Access controls on DS2 may be insufficient or there may be vulnerabilities in the DS2→P2 data flow.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as a reasonable node for disclosure threats in DataStore context

title: Linkability of Geofencing Notifications
description: The geofencing engine could link multiple arrival/departure notifications to the same user, enabling tracking of movement patterns across different zones over time.
assumptions: Notifications are associated with identifiable user accounts and timestamps are precise enough to correlate movements.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for linkability threats; confidence in applicability is high given the nature of location-based notifications.

title: Identification via Geofencing Alerts
description: The arrival/departure notifications could be used to identify specific users entering or exiting defined zones, potentially revealing sensitive location information.
assumptions: Notifications contain or can be correlated with user identifiers, and the external entity has access to this information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for identification threats; confidence in applicability is high.

title: Disclosure of Location Data to External Entity
description: The geofencing engine could disclose user location information (arrival/departure notifications) to the external entity without proper authorization or consent mechanisms.
assumptions: The external entity may not have appropriate privacy safeguards, or the data sharing lacks proper user consent.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for disclosure threats; confidence in applicability is high given the Process->ExternalEntity flow.

title: Non-compliance with Privacy Regulations
description: The geofencing notification flow could violate privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA) if location data is shared with external entities without proper legal basis, user consent, or data minimization.
assumptions: The system operates under jurisdictions with strict privacy laws, and the data sharing may not have adequate legal safeguards.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Nc.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for non-compliance threats; confidence in applicability is moderate as it depends on specific regulatory context.

title: Parent identity linked to child profile data
description: The parent's identity can be linked to the child's personal information (name, DOB, school) and geofence zones through the registration process, potentially enabling tracking of the child's location and activities via the parent's account.
assumptions: The system stores parent-child relationship data that can be used to link identities

title: Child's personal information disclosed to unauthorized parties
description: The child's sensitive personal data (name, DOB, school) and geofence zones could be disclosed to unauthorized third parties through the registration flow, violating privacy expectations for minors.
assumptions: Data transmitted from EE1 to P1 may be intercepted or accessed by unauthorized entities

title: Unauthorized account creation or profile manipulation
description: An unauthorized individual could usurp the parent's identity to create a child profile or manipulate geofence zones, potentially leading to false location tracking or privacy violations.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may be insufficient to verify parent identity

title: Child data disclosed during processing
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) may disclose the child's profile information and geofence zones to unauthorized systems or third parties during processing, storage, or transmission.
assumptions: P1 may have inadequate access controls or data sharing policies

title: Non-compliance with children's privacy regulations
description: The system may fail to comply with privacy regulations (e.g., COPPA, GDPR-K) regarding collection and processing of children's personal data during the registration flow.
assumptions: System may not implement required consent mechanisms or data minimization practices

title: Unnecessary Storage of Sensitive Child Profile Data
description: The backend stores child profile data which may include sensitive personal information. This raises concerns about data minimality - is all this data strictly required for the intended functionality?
assumptions: Child profile data contains personally identifiable information that may not be necessary for all app features
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [3] about data disclosure and minimality principle

title: Implicit Disclosure Through Geofence Metadata
description: Geofence zone data may reveal implicit information about family routines, locations, and movements through metadata patterns, even if explicit location data is not directly disclosed
assumptions: Geofence patterns can be analyzed to infer sensitive behavioral information
uncertainty_note: Dd.1.2 represents implicit disclosure through metadata/derived data as described in context [3]

title: Identifiability of Stored Account and Child Data
description: Account and child profile data stored in DS2 may be directly identifiable, creating privacy risks if accessed by unauthorized parties
assumptions: Account and child profile data contains PII that can identify individuals
uncertainty_note: I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for identifiability threats at Process→DataStore boundary

title: Data Integrity Risk for Geofence Zone Data
description: Geofence zone data could be tampered with, potentially affecting safety features or access controls that rely on accurate location boundaries
assumptions: Geofence data is used for safety-critical or access-control purposes
uncertainty_note: D.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for data integrity threats at Process→DataStore boundary

title: Linkability of child's location data to specific individual
description: Location data transmitted from child's device to Mobile App Backend can be linked to the specific child, enabling tracking of movements and patterns over time.
assumptions: Location data is transmitted with sufficient precision to identify the child's movements

title: Identifiability of child's location through map visualization
description: When location data is displayed on a map, it can reveal the child's identity, home address, school, and frequent locations, making the child identifiable to unauthorized observers.
assumptions: Map visualization includes sufficient detail to infer sensitive locations

title: Unauthorized disclosure of child's location history
description: Location history data may be disclosed to unauthorized parties through improper access controls, data breaches, or excessive sharing with third parties.
assumptions: Location history is stored and potentially accessible beyond authorized parent access

title: Excessive location data collection beyond current location need
description: Collecting full location history when only current location is requested violates data minimization principles, as historical data may not be necessary for the stated purpose.
assumptions: Parent requests current location but system collects historical data

title: GDPR compliance issues with child location data processing
description: Processing location data of a child (likely under 16) may violate GDPR requirements for special category data, consent mechanisms, and data protection by design.
assumptions: Child is a minor subject to GDPR protections
uncertainty_note: Assuming child is under GDPR age threshold; severity depends on actual age and consent mechanisms

title: Linkability of Location History to Identity
description: Stored location history can be linked to the parent's identity through the map/history view, potentially revealing patterns of movement, routines, and sensitive locations visited.
assumptions: The system associates location data with user identity; the view is accessible to authorized parties.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for linkability threats; citation based on general methodology knowledge.

title: Identification via Location Patterns
description: Location history data can be used to identify the parent's identity or infer their presence at specific locations, especially when combined with timestamps and movement patterns.
assumptions: Location data is stored with sufficient granularity; the backend has access to this data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for identification threats; citation based on general methodology knowledge.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location History
description: Location history data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties if access controls are insufficient, potentially revealing sensitive personal information about the parent's movements and habits.
assumptions: Access controls exist but may have vulnerabilities; the backend retrieves data without proper authentication/authorization checks.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for disclosure threats; citation based on general methodology knowledge.

title: Usurpation of Parent's Location Data Access
description: An attacker could potentially impersonate the parent to access their location history, either by exploiting authentication weaknesses or by gaining unauthorized access to the backend system.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms exist but may be vulnerable; the backend processes location data requests.
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for usurpation threats; citation based on general methodology knowledge.

title: Parent identity linked with child location data
description: When the parent invites a secondary guardian, the system may link the parent's identity with the child's location data, creating a privacy risk where the parent's association with the child's location is exposed.
assumptions: The system tracks which parent initiated the guardian invitation and associates this with the location data being shared.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 based on general linkability methodology; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Parent identified as location data sharer
description: The parent's identity may be revealed through the invitation mechanism, identifying them as the party sharing the child's location with a secondary guardian.
assumptions: The invitation process requires parent authentication and identity confirmation.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 based on general identification methodology; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Child location disclosed to unauthorized guardian
description: The mobile app backend may disclose the child's location to a secondary guardian without proper authorization or consent verification, potentially exposing sensitive location data to unintended parties.
assumptions: The system may not adequately verify the guardian's authorization or the parent's explicit consent before sharing location data.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 based on general disclosure methodology; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Excessive location data retained for guardian access
description: The mobile app backend may retain more location data than necessary for the secondary guardian's access, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: The system may store historical location data beyond what is needed for the guardian to view the child's current or recent location.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on general data minimization methodology; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Guardian account compromised enabling location access
description: If the secondary guardian's account is compromised, the attacker could access the child's location data through the guardian's authorized access.
assumptions: The guardian account has access to the child's location data, and account security is not robust.
uncertainty_note: Using U.1.1 based on general usurpation methodology; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Location data disclosed to unauthorized parties
description: The backend shares the child's live location with the secondary guardian, creating a risk that this sensitive data could be further disclosed to unauthorized third parties if the guardian mishandles or leaks the information.
assumptions: The guardian may not have proper safeguards in place to protect the location data from further unauthorized sharing.

title: Location data linked with other personal information
description: The secondary guardian could potentially link the child's live location data with other information they possess, creating a more detailed profile of the child's movements and habits.
assumptions: The guardian may have access to other data sources that could be correlated with the location information.

title: Child's whereabouts identified through location data
description: Live location data can directly identify the child's current whereabouts, potentially revealing sensitive information about their daily routine, school, or home location.
assumptions: Location data inherently contains identifying information about the child's physical presence.

title: Unauthorized access to location data by impostor guardian
description: An unauthorized person could potentially impersonate the secondary guardian and gain access to the child's live location data, compromising the child's safety and privacy.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may not be robust enough to prevent unauthorized access.

title: Potential violation of privacy regulations
description: Sharing a child's live location with an external entity may violate data protection regulations (e.g., GDPR, COPPA) that require explicit consent and appropriate safeguards for children's personal data.
assumptions: Regulatory requirements for children's location data sharing may not be fully met.

title: Analytics data disclosure to unauthorized third parties
description: Advertising/analytics partner may share or sell the aggregated usage and engagement data to additional third parties beyond the intended scope, potentially exposing user behavior patterns to entities without proper consent or legal basis.
assumptions: Partner has business incentives to monetize data beyond the agreed scope; data may be re-identifiable when combined with other datasets.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a general disclosure node; specific partner contract terms would determine exact risk level.

title: Regulatory non-compliance in data sharing
description: Sharing aggregated analytics with external advertising partner may violate GDPR, CCPA, or other privacy regulations if data is not properly anonymized, if consent was not obtained, or if data minimization principles are not followed.
assumptions: User consent for analytics sharing may not cover third-party advertising partners; aggregated data may still contain quasi-identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Specific regulatory requirements depend on user location and data characteristics; tree node Nc.1.1 is a general non-compliance node.

title: Linkability of aggregated analytics across datasets
description: Even aggregated usage and engagement data may be linkable when combined with other datasets held by the advertising partner or other entities, potentially enabling re-identification of individual users through correlation attacks.
assumptions: Advertising partners typically have access to multiple data sources; aggregation may not be sufficient to prevent linkage when combined with other datasets.
uncertainty_note: Risk depends on aggregation granularity and partner's data ecosystem; tree node L.1.1 is a general linkability node.

title: Location data enables child identification
description: The child's current location data in the check-in/SOS message can be used to identify the child's physical whereabouts and potentially link to their identity.
assumptions: Location data is precise enough to identify the child's location

title: Location data disclosed to unauthorized parties
description: The child's location data could be disclosed to unauthorized third parties through the mobile app backend or during transmission.
assumptions: The system may not have proper access controls

title: Excessive location data collection
description: The check-in/SOS message may collect more precise location data than necessary for the intended purpose of parent notification.
assumptions: The system collects GPS coordinates rather than approximate location

title: Child identity usurpation in SOS message
description: An unauthorized person could potentially send a check-in/SOS message on behalf of the child, impersonating them.
assumptions: The system lacks proper authentication for SOS messages
